Daniel’s two snippets are a neat way to surface a big, usually hidden design choice: do you *gate* work on an introspective “focus score,” or do you *default* into work and only retreat when reality proves you can’t? The central weakness in policy 1 is its dependence on `assessMyFocus()`—an oracle that is likely both noisy and strategically biased. If the reward for “low focus” is an immediately gratifying game, the assessment function will tend to drift toward self-justification (“I’m not focused enough yet”) rather than measurement; that’s less a moral failing than a predictable Goodhart’s-law failure mode in self-tracking. Policy 2 avoids that by making “study” the default path, but it smuggles in a different assumption: that failure to focus will manifest as a clean, detectable exception. In practice it’s often a slow degradation—reading the same paragraph three times, tab-switching, half-studying—that never throws `CannotFocus` but still burns time.

A second blind spot is that both policies treat “game for 30 minutes” as a neutral, reusable recovery primitive. That may be true for some people, but many will find it creates a ratchet: games are engineered for rapid feedback and variable rewards, which can make returning to low-stimulation study harder, not easier. This is where Daniel’s framing brushes up against behaviorist reinforcement schedules and modern attention engineering; if the fallback is too rewarding, the whole loop becomes a training regime for avoidance. The classic alternative in productivity lore—structured, low-friction breaks and timeboxed work units (e.g., the [Pomodoro Technique](https://francescocirillo.com/pages/pomodoro-technique))—isn’t just “more wholesome”; it’s a different control strategy that reduces the incentive to misclassify your internal state.

If Daniel wanted to sharpen the model, the missing piece is a higher-level scheduler and clearer termination criteria: *what counts as a “study” unit, when does the loop end, and what evidence matters—felt focus or produced work?* In control-theory terms, both policies are pure reactive controllers with a single actuator (game) and no notion of accumulating fatigue, diminishing returns, or next-day spillovers. A more robust design would treat focus as a budget that can be replenished (sleep, food, movement, social reset), distinguish “can’t focus” from “task is ill-specified,” and make the fallback proportional and reversible—so recovery doesn’t become the primary equilibrium.
